Madam Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43 I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
In light of the grossly insufficient amount of funding available to meet current Farm Credit Corporation loan demands which is threatening the viability of thousands of farmers, particularly the young and those starting new operations, and given the failure of the government to respond in a positive way, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Shields):
That the minister take the necessary immediate steps to increase the level of funding of the Farm Credit Corporation by at least $150 million and to ensure that the lending rate not exceed the current level of 12.75 per cent.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
On Tuesday of this week the United States Secretary of Defence announced that he was seriously considering the deployment of the neutron bomb. In light of the fact that this weapon's deployment would only serve to heighten East-West tension, and in light of the fact that the neutron bomb, a weapon that destroys people but leaves buildings and property unharmed, would increase the risk of all-out nuclear war, 1 move, seconded by the hon. member for Saskatoon East (Mr. Ogle):
That this House instructs the government to join with the government of The Netherlands, which yesterday voted to reject the deployment of the neutron bomb in western Europe, and, further, that this House instructs the government to communicate this country's grave concerns regarding this matter to the government of the United States.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I too rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. A private American corporation, Satellite Business Systems, has applied to the U.S. Federal Communications Commission for permission to link its transmission services to five major Canadian cities. The minister's own department has shown that transborder data transmission will lead to re-centralization of control by multinationals over their subsidiaries and a consequent loss of jobs in Canada. The Clyne commission agrees.
I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for New Westminster-Coquitlam (Miss Jewett):
That since the proposed service will require Canadian permission, the government refuses to grant authorization for further foreign intrusion which threatens Canada's independence and telecommunications future.

Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Last night in Brandon the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), in a desperate attempt to aggrandize his own shallow self-interest, insinuated that if Westminster, the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada, seven Canadian premiers, the energy producing provinces, the editorial writers of Canada and the majority of Canadian citizens disagree with his policies, then the "Prime Minister must be doing something right".

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration

subsubtopic: MR. NIELSEN-THE CONSTITUTION-TABLING OF LETTER FROM BRITISH PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
After the point of order raised Monday by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen), I had an opportunity to read Hansard for yesterday and Monday, as he had asked me to do, in connection with the tabling of certain documents in the House. In his intervention last Tuesday, the hon. member for Yukon had informed the Chair of his intention to raise a point of order about some of the answers given by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan) during question period.
The hon. member for Yukon then alleged that several times the hon. ministers concerned had referred to or quoted long excerpts from a letter which the Prime Minister is said to have received from the United Kingdom Prime Minister, Mrs. Thatcher.
It seems to me the Standing Orders are clear about the obligation of a minister to lay upon the table a state paper from which he has already quoted. I am sure all hon. members know Citation 327 in Beauchesne's fifth edition. It is true that the hon. ministers referred to that letter during question period, put after close examination of Hansard I was unable to find a passage which appeared to me as being a direct quotation. Having consulted the precedents, may I draw the hon. members' attention to a ruling of one of my predecessors, Mr. Lamoureux, which can be found at page 9599 of Hansard for November 16, 1971, and I quote:
I have to agree with the contention that if the reference made to a public document is not, as the citation says, a quotation from that document, it would be very difficult for the Chair to rule that the document ought to be tabled.
If a document has been actually cited or quoted in debate by a minister of the Crown, it has to be tabled. If only reference is made to it, I do not see how there can be an obligation to table it.
In his remarks yesterday the hon. member for Yukon stated that the Chair had the duty to order the government to table the letter in question. He rested his argument on Citation 327 in Beauchesne's fifth edition whose relevant section reads as follows:
To be cited, a document must be quoted or specifically used to influence debate.
I confess I was somewhat surprised by this citation, so I made it my duty to check the sources on which this Section (5)

February 5, 1981
Order Paper Questions
of Beauchesne's Citation 327 might have been based. Now, the precedents of 1957 and 1975 which can be found do not mention the fact that a document is used specifically to influence debate. One might even wonder whether the Chair can determine if a document did or did not influence debate. It is an extremely difficult judgment for the Chair to make. Therefore, I must return to the first section of the citation which is itself based on a quotation of Erskine May, and which did not change in any way the fundamental rule followed until now by all my predecessors. Indeed that is the ruling made in similar circumstances by Mr. Speaker Jerome on March 4, 1975. Among other things, he said, and I quote:
Surely, a reasonable interpretation of the words "quotation from a document" must mean a quotation from the body of a document-
He then specified just what constituted quoting. And, on April 8, 1976, along the same line of thought, he added:
However, this certainly has never been held to apply to a situation in which a minister-
-as in this case-

has simply been asked a question about a document and given an answer.
Therefore an attempt to secure information based on a certain document certainly does not entail that it is necessary to table the said document.
Under the circumstances, I see no reason why my opinion should differ from that of my predecessors, and I cannot find any Standing Order under which the Prime Minister might be forced to table the document in question.

speechtext: The House resumed from Monday, December 15, 1980, consideration of the motion of Mr. Bussieres (for the Minister of Finance) that Bill C-24, to amend laws relating to fiscal transfers to the provinces, be read the second time and referred to the Committee of the Whole.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the House for waiving Standing Orders to allow me to participate for what amounts to a second time in the second reading debate on Bill C-24, respecting fiscal transfers to the provinces.
When second reading on Bill C-24 commenced on December 15 last we had some excellent contributions by the minister, the hon. member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) in particular, and by the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood (Mr. Rae). They pointed out the concerns of their respective parties with regard to this piece of legislation with its three clauses.
The first two clauses deal with what is commonly referred to as the equalization arrangements in this country. They deal with changes brought about, or made necessary, as a result of new developments in the western provinces, in particular the tremendous growth in resource revenues. These are the provinces which contain the oil and gas, which recently have gone up so much in value.
Fiscal Transfers to Provinces
We must maintain a nation with some degree of equality to each citizen, no matter where he lives, so that Canadians living in one province can enjoy services provided by the government, at a level roughly equivalent to those services provided in another province. The original motivation for equalization was, in fact, from my part of the country, from the prairies. During the twenties, thirties and, indeed, the early forties, this was an extremely impoverished part of the country-at least before Leduc. There was a great deal of resentment and bitterness felt by western Canadians until 1930 because the resources did not belong to the provinces. Then, during the 1930s, there was the depression which had such an enormous impact on the prairie provinces. It created real hardships, to the point where the province of Alberta defaulted on bonds.
During this time there was an interest by those provinces in having some fairness with respect to the taxation scheme. Corporate taxes were collected at the headquarters of companies, and those were companies which earned their incomes right across Canada from coast to coast usually had their headquarters in Toronto or Montreal. Since taxes were collected in Ontario or Quebec the western provinces had no accessibility to them. The western provinces, of course, had the same kinds of obligations, as did the eastern ones, to provide roads, hospitals and so on.
The Rowell-Sirois Commission was an outgrowth of that kind of concern and frustration. It is rather ironic to recall that the greatest objection to sharing or to any sense of equalization in those days came from the Liberal premier of Ontario, Mitch Hepburn. We did arrive, primarily as the result of the Rowell-Sirois report of 1952, although the present scheme was worked out in 1966, at an equalization scheme which has worked reasonably well. This equalization scheme is based on a fairly complicated revenue-sharing arrangement. It is a complicated formula which considers the normal types of revenues.
One of the types of revenues which is considered as part of the equalization formula is the funds raised by the provinces in offering land for exploitation of mining companies or energy companies. In the case of Alberta-and I am aware that the other two provinces are similar-in order to have a fair or even-handed approach to industry with regard to exploitation of the natural resources, the province has in place a system whereby companies offer closed bids for the right to explore a given piece of land.
As oil prices have increased and as new technology increased the prospects of further oil and gas discoveries, the price of that land increased dramatically. The price has increased to the extent that the amount of money collected by the provinces for these reports of land sales is very substantial and has thrown a tremendous skew into the equalization program, causing the federal government, with the consent of the provinces, to move this amendment which would remove those types of revenues from the equalization formula.
The second amendment to the equalization formula was probably included in the first instance simply because it makes

Fiscal Transfers to Provinces
common sense, and that is that no province with an average income higher than the national average shall be the beneficiary of equalization. We in this party-and 1 know the New Democratic Party shares the same view, as I am sure does the Liberal Party-feel strongly that the question of equalization goes to the core of what Canada is all about in a real sense. It is a tremendously complex, difficult problem, with which the nation will have to deal in the near future. Goodness knows, there are enough things threatening to tear this country apart, and to add to the current problems a major dispute over the question of equalization would, indeed, be serious.
For that reason we concur with and strongly endorse the notion of establishing a special task force on the question of equalization. In fact the hon. member for Mississauga South moved a Standing Order 43 on January 28 which was exactly to that effect, that this task force be set up. We very much welcome the acceptance of this suggestion by the government and the concurrence by the New Democratic Party. We look forward to participating in that task force, to helping broaden the understanding of the elements of equalization, not just to Parliament, but to the nation, and at least starting the process of building a newer and better way of sharing in this country which is not quite as fractious, disruptive and damaging as the sharing procedures which are being attempted through the National Energy Program.
The other aspect of today's proceedings which is absolutely vital is the question of the Public Utilities Income Tax Transfer Act. This act goes back to 1946, but in its current form it goes back to 1966. It rebates to the provinces 95 per cent of the income tax collected from privately owned utilities. The reason for the act is very simple. It is based on the fundamental principle which must underline all federal taxation, namely, that taxpayers of equal circumstance, no matter where they are located in this country, should be taxed equally by the federal government. The tax system should not have built into it a bias which says that if one happens to live in this or that province one shall pay less or more federal tax.
PUITTA, the Public Utilities Income Tax Transfer Act, put into the system this kind of fairness because of the development of provincially-owned utilities which, because of the BNA Act, are non-taxable by the federal government and which, as a result, caused a distortion. The users of publicly-owned utilities were not in fact paying the corporate taxes which users of services provided by privately-owned utilities were paying. Simply stated, it was absolutely inequitable.
PUITTA removed that inequity. Hence, we are in the situation today where we have agreed that we will leave PUITTA in place. I am not sure what my reaction should be, whether I should be thankful, happy or mad. It is rather like being faced with a robber who, by use of argument, force or some other means, you convince not to rob you. What should one's feelings be at the end? Is one suppose to be grateful to the potential robber because he did not commit the robbery? The reality is that no fair-minded Canadian could accept the repeal of PUITTA, nor could this party.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-24 is an act to amend certain arrangements made over the years relating to fiscal transfers to the provinces. It is an attempt to deal with certain imbalances and anomalies that have arisen within the established equalization formula as a result of the significant increases in revenues that the energy producing provinces have experienced since 1973, anomalies such as that which has put Ontario, at present a have province, in a category where it qualifies for equalization payments. To the extent that this bill deals with something that is as fundamental to Canadian federalism as equalization, so fundamental in fact that the principle of equalization payments is to be enshrined in the Constitution, this must not be regarded as a minor piece of legislation.
We are dealing with a principle that goes back to the Rowell-Sirois Commission in pre-World War II days which progressively developed into the perception and consensus that it was the federal government's responsibility to bring all the provinces up to a common level of revenue and services.
The problem we now seem to be facing with respect to the question of resources revenue is twofold.
I wonder if I could have a little quiet on the other side of the House, Mr. Speaker. I can hardly hear myself think.
The resource revenues place greater demands on the federal government, as there is a higher level of revenue for all provinces to be brought up to and secondly, to the extent that the government has not had adequate access to these new revenues it has experienced difficulty in affording the resulting increase in the cost of equalization.
This bill is one in a series of attempts to deal with this problem. On the one hand it reduces those revenues that the federal government must calculate into the equalization formula and thus saves the government money. On the other hand it allows the producing provinces to build up such things as heritage funds, funds which we in this party acknowledge as necessary to the future of the economies of those provinces which now depend on rich, but nevertheless depleting, nonrenewable resources.
In all these manoeuvres there is, as always, somebody who ends up with the short end of the stick. As the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood (Mr. Rae) said in debate on this same bill on December 15, 1980, it is neither the federal government nor the producing provinces which lose out as a result of these changes; it is the people of the have-not provinces who lose as a result of them. In this way it can be said that we are actually moving away from the equalization ideal, if the essence of equalization is indeed to help the have not provinces to maintain a level of revenue and services equal to some national standard. What is at stake here is the idea of national standards, an idea which I will deal with more fully
Fiscal Transfers to Provinces
when I speak of federal-provincial fiscal transfers as they pertain to health care in Canada.
This is why we in the New Democratic Party have called for a parliamentary task force on equalization. In the intergovernmental negotiations that will undoubtedly take place, Members of Parliament, representative of and concerned about all regions and provinces of Canada, should have a chance to study and to make recommendations about the way the imminent restructuring of equalization should take place for the benefit of Canadians, and not just for the benefit of the more powerful. Ways must be found to solve whatever problems there are, ways which do not endanger the standard of services available to Canadians in the have-not provinces, or wherever they may live. Canadians who have lost what the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood has called "the game of geological roulette" must be assured a full share of the quality of life which is available in Canada.
In this context I should like to speak about the problem of those federal-provincial transfer payments which fall under the description of the Established Programs Financing Act, that arrangement between the federal government and the provinces which was arrived at in 1977 and which defines federal contributions for hospital insurance, the Medicare Act, post secondary education, and extended health care services.
At the time of its passing the NDP opposed this arrangement for reasons that merit repetition at this time. We were worried about several things. In addition to the obvious unconditional nature of the revenues transferred to the provinces via the transfer of tax points, there was a dangerous vagueness about the extent to which the revenue transferred to the provinces via the basic cash payment could be expected to be conditional upon this money being spent on the purposes for which it was intended. We were worried about the maintenance of a level of services consistent with the potential combination of federal money and unabated provincial support for these programs. A transitional additional payment was thrown in by the federal government for the sake of the poorer provinces. They would receive transitional cash payments equal to what was needed to bring them up to the national average. This was in recognition of the fact that richer provinces would receive more revenue from the tax point transfers than poorer ones.
Furthermore, the $7.63 per capita part of the basic cash payment which was included by the federal government in lieu of the termination of the agreement called the revenue guarantee, now appears to have been correctly perceived by the provinces as unconditional, if Justice Hall's conclusions are to be heeded in this matter. This points to the vagueness of a poorly worded and poorly conceived document.
Without getting into any more detail of what is a very complicated arrangement, the important thing to notice about all this is that the Established Programs Financing Act has resulted in a serious lowering of provincial contributions to health care, on a percentage basis. The result of this has been a serious cutback in services and quality of care available to Canadians who live in the provinces governed by those who

February 5, 1981
Fiscal Transfers to Provinces
have seen their new found economy in health care spending or direct federal government input into health care, as an opportunity to save money. There was an element of restraint in the 1977 arrangements both federally and provincially. Provincial governments would not have to spend a dollar to get a dollar as they did under the former 50-50 cost-sharing arrangement. There would be an incentive for competency. But there was also supposed to be freedom for innovation and expansion of health care as provincial governments used their new found freedom from federal strictures to respond more adequately to the needs of their people. The question then becomes one of whether the provinces have lived up to the moral as well as the administrative bargain that was reached in 1977.
With respect to individual provinces, one's judgment on the extent to which they have lived up to the bargain will in all likelihood be a combination of statistical and financial evidence, combined with a general impression of health care services in the respective provinces and observations about whether people, with respect to provinces, perceive their health care system to be in a state of relative decline.
I note this combined idea of measurement because the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin), when asked by myself and others in question period, time after time, as to what she intends to do about delinquent provinces such as Alberta, Manitoba and Ontario, is fond of bringing up the province of Saskatchewan. This is supposed to be a bold political stroke on her part, or so it would seem from the self-satisfied smile which envelopes her when she devastates us like that. The Liberals, of course, have the dubious luxury of not having any provincial governments to speak about.
The fact remains that, statistically, the Saskatchewan government is shown in a document prepared by the Liberal finance department to be one of the few provinces where provincial per capita contribution has gone up since 1977 and where it can be said that all federal increases have been passed on to residents in the form of expanded health care program funding.
Further, it should be noted for the minister's benefit that the people of Saskatchewan have not risen up in righteous anger like the people of other provinces. Indeed, the Canadian Health Coalition cannot get anything going in Saskatchewan because health care is not an issue there. The government of that province is concerned about health care, and the people know it. Because health care in Saskatchewan is supplemented and complemented by other social programs of a preventive nature, it reduces the need for purely crisis-oriented medicine. Let us be done with the cheap shot misrepresentations about Saskatchewan which have been popularized in this House by the Minister of National Health and Welfare and her cohort in this, the hon. member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie), and let us look at two of the greatest transgressors in the deterioration of medicare which Canada has experienced since block funding was introduced. I am speaking, of course, about Manitoba and Ontario.
In Manitoba, according to the same document prepared for the Department of Finance to which I referred earlier, federal funding has increased by 18 per cent to 19 per cent while the provincial government manages to contribute 13 to 16 per cent less than it did in constant dollars in 1975-76. A view of aggregated health function spending shows a growth in the federal share from 45 per cent before established programs financing to 52 per cent today, while the provincial per capita contribution has gone down from $163.45 in 1975-76 to $142.09 in 1979-80. The downward trend was overcome only once in that period, in 1976-77 when it went up, not uncoincidentally, in the last year of the NDP government in Manitoba.
These are the statistics, damning enough, but the human reality is far more significant. Tired, overworked nurses, underpaid and understaffed maintenance personnel, cranky doctors, people waiting on stretchers in halls for hours in order to be admitted to emergency or in order to have their laundry changed on Monday mornings because they no longer hire people on the weekends, postponed elective surgery, the aged, the infirm and chronically ill being sent home prematurely because of a lack of space, and a general lack of confidence, are some of the problems.
The people of Manitoba used to take pride in their health care system. Over the years they elected members of Parliament who were part of the fight for medicare, such as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) who fought for medicare against the reactionary and insensitive machinations of the Conservatives and the usual procrastination, reluctance and general lack of conviction characteristic of the Liberal party. The people of Manitoba will no doubt take steps to restore their pride in the way they look after each other come the next general election in Manitoba.
Now let us look at Ontario, a province which, because it never had a New Democratic government, has even more structural attacks on the principles of medicare than Manitoba. In Ontario, atrocities like widespread extra billing, hospital charges and premiums are piled on top of the kinds of things which Manitobans have had to put up with in the last few years. What an irony that, in one of the richest provinces in Canada, the political culture has not yet matured to the point where people in Ontario do not have to pay for their health care through the regressive mechanism of premiums.
Statistically, according to the document I have been referring to throughout, the federal share of health care funding in Ontario has gone from 41.5 per cent before established programs financing to 52.4 per cent at this time. Real provincial expenditures have decreased by 3 per cent while, in addition to federal increases, the people of Ontario have experienced a 27 per cent increase in what they paid through premiums.
Using figures submitted to the Hall commission, which were approved by the government of Ontario, we see that while increasing provincial per capita expenditures by a paltry 3.6 per cent, the government of Premier Bill Davis has managed to reduce its own funding by 29.3 per cent amid real federal increases of 27 per cent and real premium increases of 27 per cent. What, pray tell, are the people of Ontario paying for?
February 5, 1981

The "big blue machine" turns out to be a reference to the way in which the health of the people of Ontario is being choked off by the ham-handed and blind, stupid restraint of the Progressive Conservative Party of Ontario.
What is the answer? Under the present system the federal government, because it gave up the carrot in 1977 and has only the stick, has the threat to cut off funding. It is a very serious threat unless, of course, you are Alberta and have the political cheek to say, as the government of Alberta did the other day, that you are prepared to do without federal funding in order to get your own way and keep on being a province where extra billing and opting out take place at intolerable levels. Little Peter has threatened to run away from home.
The more serious question is what has happened to the Minister of National Health and Welfare who once threatened the provinces. She now challenges the NDP to recommend the same thing. When we complained about the state of medicare in some provinces, she challenges us to recommend this as if it were something that she in her new found wisdom had never thought of.
Justice Hall recommended against any withdrawal of federal funding. He recommended against what the Minister of National Health and Welfare threatened to do so many times in the last two election campaigns. We are prepared to accept the wisdom of this judgment by Justice Hall, as long as it is accompanied by a commitment on the part of the federal government to change the Established Programs Financing Act in such a way as to make the provinces more accountable for the maintenance of certain national standards.
We suggest the introduction of a new form of 50-50 cost sharing. It would preserve the notion of flexibility while reconstituting health care and post-secondary education in Canada as a joint-federal-provincial responsibility, something we act together on, not something the federal government throws money at and then forgets about.
What we in this party are afraid of, and what I now warn the Canadian people about, particularly those in the poorer provinces or in provinces where the governments are hostile to medicare is that the federal government, instead of trying to rebuild and re-establish a co-operative federalist approach to health care and post-secondary education, will try to get out from under what remains of its responsibility in this area.
Contrary to the centralizing image of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on important social and practical matters such as health care, he has literally given away the store. On economic matters he seems to want power, only not to use it. He idly contemplates power while our economy falls apart for lack of planning and direction.
Let me return to the topic of medicare. We suggest the federal government should not compound the error of most provincial governments by negotiating the renewal of Established Programs Financing, as it must be renewed in the coming year, with a view to saving money. The goal should be to stimulate provinces to greater responsibility for medicare
Fiscal Transfers to Provinces
and for the federal government to maintain its sense of responsibility over health care.
One of the reasons the federal government has given in the last little while about its need to save money in respect of federal-provincial transfer payments, particularly in the statement in the budget as to how the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) looks forward to and anticipates saving money in the upcoming renegotiation of federal-provincial fiscal arrangements, is the revenue squeeze the government has been in of late.
Indeed it would be ironic if, at the same time the Liberal government was moving to solve the revenue problem, as it did in respect of its recent National Energy Program by having accrued to it more of the revenues coming from resources in this country, it was doing so by trying to get out of its responsibilities in those areas where Canadians have traditionally looked to the federal government for leadership.
In 1977, when the present arrangement of Established Programs Financing was brought into being against the criticisms and opposition of the NDP, we were warned by the father of medicare, Mr. Douglas, the then hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands, just what was involved in this particular rearrangement of the federal government's responsibility in health care. Let me conclude by quoting him as follows:
The fact is that this bill will destroy the very thing which since 1945 successive federal governments have been seeking to establish, namely, national standards for the people of Canada by which the federal government, through equalization payments and sharing the cost of programs on a 50-50 basis, could assure that a little province like Prince Edward Island would be able to give its people services that are comparable to the wealthiest province of Canada, the province of Ontario.
He went on to state:
This country was founded by men and women who had a dream that it was possible to bring together diverse groups of people with different cultural backgrounds, who spoke different languages but who could live together in a spirit of tolerance and good will. They believed it was possible that the strong would help the weak, that the wealthy provinces would help succor the poorer provinces and that we would build a standard of Canadian living which would be our pride. If we fail to do that, then we are not worthy of those in whose footsteps we follow.
My plea to the government and the Canadian people is the same as that of Mr. Douglas at the time. We should make up our minds that we will not allow the apathy which seems to be creeping into the federal government in respect of the attitudes of provincial governments toward our health care, to destroy the Canadian dream, of which medicare is an integral part.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was very glad to hear the hon. member for Win-nipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) quote Mr. Douglas at the end of his speech because those very generous words somehow offset his mean and partisan attack on the attitude of some provinces and even of the central government with regard to the financing of certain established programs which, by the way, are not affected by this bill.
6928

February 5, 1981
Fiscal Transfers to Provinces
The purpose of this bill which was rather well explained, if I may say so, by the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre), is to amend two statutory programs. The first one deals with the equalization payments authorized under the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements and Established Programs Financing Act, 1977, and the second with the payments made under the Public Utility Income Tax Transfer Act. It will be recalled, that the equalization program is intended to transfer enough revenue to the poorer provinces to help them provide a reasonable level of service to the public without having to impose on taxpayers levels of taxation which would be greater than their ability to pay. I would like to indicate that the equalization program is based on a province's ability to provide these services. For the purposes of the program, the revenues that each province would get through average levels of taxation, according to its own tax base, are assessed and its future revenues, in cases where the province is above average, are adjusted upwards. This is a way of ensuring that the provinces have sufficient financial resources to finance public services.
The equalization program is one of the most important programs implemented by the federal government. I want to assure the House that the government is as firmly committed as ever to this program. As the hon. member indicated, it is such an important program that it was examined during the constitutional discussions with a view to including the equalization principle in the Canadian Constitution. The fact that the amounts paid out under this program are quite considerable clearly shows the federal government's commitment to this principle.
The basis of the equalization formula is a revenue fund from which the provinces can draw. As the bill indicates, the revenues are generated by oil and natural gas and in particular they come from the sale of Crown leases and reservations on oil and natural gas lands. The reason why these two sources of revenue are removed from the revenue fund is that since 1975-76 especially there has been a very rapid increase of these oil revenues which throws off balance so to speak the fund made of these various sources of revenues.
Therefore, over a two-year period, the revenues generated by the sale of Crown leases on oil and natural gas lands will be removed for purposes of equalization. 1 would also like to indicate that as a result of representations made in the course of the debate on this bill, the government decided to remove clause 3 of the bill on reimbursements under the Public Utility Income Tax Transfer Act. It has repeatedly been indicated during the debate-and the hon. member for Calgary Centre has reaffirmed it-that the financial consequences of this bill would be limited but that they would affect especially the province of Alberta. I should like to point out that it would also affect Newfoundland and Prince Edward Island. Many organizations, consumer groups, Members of Parliament, even the Minister of State for Economic Development, Senator
Olson, and my hon. colleague, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy), have strongly argued that this provision should be withdrawn from the bill. Therefore, I am pleased to inform the House that as a result of those representations the government will drop Clause 3 from this bill.
Apparently we will have to proceed in the following manner: when the bill reaches Committee of the Whole and the Chair calls Clause 3, the government will vote against it.
That change will not affect the two other provisions of the bill dealing with equalization payments namely the revenue and the average personal income for the three years on the basis of which no fiscal equalization payment may be paid to a province.
We also heard the leader of the government in the House suggest that a task force be set up to study the 1977 act on fiscal transfers, as well as the Canadian welfare system and equalization program. I have a feeling that the task force could come up with interesting suggestions before we renegotiate those various programs with the provinces. I am confident the hon. members who are appointed to the force will work constructively and positively in an effort to help the government-through those programs-to communicate better with the provinces.
I should like, in closing, to thank very briefly the House leaders of the opposition parties, as well as the critics of those parties, the government House leader, the hon. member for Calgary Centre and the hon. member for Broadview-Green-wood (Mr. Rae), for their co-operation which resulted in a speedy passage of the bill this afternoon.
I think this week could be declared parliamentary efficiency week since we completed study of the income tax bill yesterday and we shall proceed with third reading of Bill C-24 within a matter of minutes. Therefore, I thank all the hon. members for their co-operation.

speechtext: The House resumed, from Friday, January 30, 1981, consideration of the motion of Mr. Bussieres (for the Minister of Finance) that Bill C-59, to provide supplementary borrowing authority, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the third time in little over a year that the House has been faced with a borrowing authority bill; this is the second borrowing authority bill presented to the House in this session of Parliament. The House will recall that in July of this year the government was given authority to borrow $12 billion. That was only eight months ago. So far in this fiscal year the government has borrowed from the public in general, on the open market and elsewhere, a total of $9 billion of new money. That is the figure, according to the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), as of last January 15. Obviously there has been some borrowing since then, but in his statement the minister estimated he would need another approximate $3 billion to meet his requirements for this fiscal year.
When we went into this fiscal year the government had outstanding borrowing capacity, which had not lapsed, of $2.9 billion. To the $2.9 billion borrowing authority of the government at the beginning of the fiscal year one would normally add the $12 billion authorized in July, to give the government a total borrowing capacity in this fiscal year of $14.9 billion. As of December 15 the government had used up $9 billion of its $14.9 billion borrowing authority. At that point it still had $5.9 billion, and I remind hon. members of the minister's statement with respect to Bill C-54. Unfortunately for the government, Bill C-54 was altered by House order, so his speech on that bill was actually off the topic. The minister indicated that we had $5.9 billion left, and of that amount he anticipated he would need only $3 billion to the end of the fiscal year. That would leave the government at the end of March, 1981, with $2.9 billion of borrowing authority.
The government is coming to us and saying, in addition to the $2.9 billion of borrowing authority, that it needs an additional $14 billion. In other words, the government wants us to give it a blank cheque to borrow a total of $16.9 billion in the period ending March 31, 1982, which is more than the government has shown it needs for this fiscal year. Indeed it is significantly more than the government has shown in its budget for next fiscal year.
Borrowing Authority
If one is to examine the budget presented by the minister last October 28, hon. members will note on table 1 the amount required for borrowing. Hon. members will also note the deficit in the revenue and expenditures on a national accounts basis. The deficit for the year 1981-1982 set out in table 3 is $10,060 million, and the note to that table indicates that it is an average amount. However, if we go back to the summary of transactions, we find that the amount the government will require, according to its budget figures, is no more than $11 billion. On the one hand, the government is saying that it will have borrowing authority for $16.9 billion, but on the other hand the government tells us in that fiscal year it will need only $11 billion. The House is being asked to approve the borrowing of $5.9 billion more than the government budgetary requirements indicate. This is an unconscionable request of this House of Commons. There is no way that responsible Members of Parliament, responsible as Parliament is to control the public purse, can in any conscience grant this request for the right to borrow money. I say, "No way". The government's figures do not add up. The government does not need that much money; there is no real requirement for it. The government is asking this House to approve $5.9 billion in borrowing authority over the maximum amount the government could possibly need, that is, in accordance with its budget.
The government tells us its budgets are right and it is capable of managing people's affairs; that is what we hear. The minister was in Toronto the other day talking about his monetary and fiscal policy, his policy of gradualism and his policy of restraint. We know about this government's restraint attitude. It is so restrained that the government is asking us to give it $5.9 billion more than it even wants in its budget! Is that restraint?
Let us look at some of the government's problems. It is only when we are responsible and pay attention to what is ongoing on a fiscal basis in this country that we, as Members of Parliament, earn our pay and earn the respect of the citizens of Canada. The problems of the government financing are simply horrendous.
Today, again, interest rates determined by the Bank of Canada stayed at 17.11 per cent. Some would ask, "Well, isn't it marvellous the government is able to keep interest rates at the same level of 17.11 per cent as it did last week?" But, the wire service report this afternoon, after the Bank of Canada's auction of treasury bills, indicated that the Bank of Canada so interfered with the bid on treasury bills this week that it was able to keep the 17.11 per cent rate from going to where it should have gone, that is, to 17.30 per cent. We will know exactly what happened at five o'clock this afternoon when the Bank of Canada report comes out, but it is clear from the information leaked so far that the Bank of Canada again cranked up the printing press, bought up treasury bills and increased the amount of government monetizing in order to keep the interest rate where, I ask hon. members? It kept it at 17.11 per cent, but that is the highest rate the Bank of Canada has ever had in its entire history. Is that managing?

February 5, 1981
Borrowing Authority
The disaster of it is this: we owe the government, as of last week, a net debt-and I am talking net, net, net debt-of well in excess of $80 billion. The worst of that net, net, net debt is that most of it, a good half of it, is what any accountant would call a current liability.
Every week the government goes to the financial markets and must borrow at least $1 billion. In some cases it borrows up to $1,500 million every week. That is just to roll over its treasury bills and pick up an extra $100 or $200 million to cover its deficit. It is a weekly performance. Those treasury bills are written for 90 days, 91 days or 182 days. They are short-term loans. They are due. They are what an accountant would call a current liability. Of that current liability, in the statement of last week, the government owed $20.9 billion on treasury bills alone.
In addition to that, the government owes on Canada Savings Bonds not quite $17 billion. I want to speak for a moment about that form of debt, namely, that in connection with Canada Savings Bonds. As you know, Mr. Speaker, those bonds can be cashed at any time without notice. Therefore, they are a current liability of the government. Today we have a Canada Savings Bond interest rate of 11.5 per cent. We all know by looking at every bank advertisement across the country that one can go today to any savings bank, chartered bank or trust company in Canada and receive 13 per cent on one savings account. We all know that guaranteed investment certificates are being marketed today at 13.5 per cent, sometimes 13.75 per cent. Some smaller institutions offer interest on those certificates even up to 14 per cent.
We all know, if we have any intelligence at all, that the forward outlook for interest rates this year indicate that interest rates will remain high for the balance of the year. When one looks at the bid price of commercial paper running six or nine months down the road, and when one looks at one year paper, the rates quoted on the commercial market are close to 15 per cent, if not higher. That must indicate something.
It must indicate that the market believes interest rates are likely to remain in the 15 per cent range, at least for the balance of the year, while the Bank of Canada rate today, by its manipulations, is only 17.11 per cent. The interest rate forecasts indicate that at no time this year will the Bank of Canada rate, to wit, the rate at which the Government of Canada can borrow money, be below 15 per cent. That is a horror! We in this country have been faced with interest rates in the 17 per cent range on the Bank of Canada basis for eight weeks now, and there is no prospect of those rates declining. We are talking about that rate when we talk about government debt, money which it must borrow.
The Minister of Finance indicated in the budget that his cost of carrying borrowed money for this fiscal year would be $10.25 billion, but that projection was made on October 28 when interest rates were 5 per cent to 7 per cent less than today. That projection is wrong by a full four months. It
indicates that the government's budgetary handling of debt costs is wrong. What I am afraid of-and what a number of members on this side and surely members opposite are afraid of-is that under this bill we will be giving the government borrowing authority so that it can borrow money to pay the interest on the money borrowed at the high interest rates that this high-interest government has created.
When we get into this whole problem we must look very seriously at where we are going in Canada. The late John Diefenbaker said, "Where are we going, where are we going?"
1 should like to read into the record the remarks of Richard Thomson, chief executive officer of the Toronto-Dominion Bank, at the annual meeting of its shareholders. He said:
The high level of Canadian inflation and the expectation of it continuing at even higher levels set a floor on Canadian interest rates as the Bank of Canada sought to maintain Canadian interest rates above the rate of inflation.
He went on to say:
As United States rates jumped to new highs, the Canadian authorities, particularly the Bank of Canada, had the option either to increase Canadian interest rates or to witness a decline in the Canadian exchange rate.
The government, in its management, decided to keep interest rates high in Canada so that it could keep the dollar high. Well, let us look at the dollar for a moment. It has not done very well recently. At noon today it was only at 83.56 cents in New York.
The government has succeeded in keeping the interest rates exceptionally high. The disaster of that is that the bulk of the borrowing in Canada is being done by the government itself. So, when we on this side of the House talk about the terror of high interest rates to people who hold mortgages-and it is a terror-and when we talk of high interest rates affecting consumers-and it is really hurting them-and when we talk of high interest rates destroying business, particularly small business, the fact of the matter is that we are all paying for the disaster of high interest rates because we are all Canadians. We are all stuck with paying this horrendous rate on what amounts to current account borrowing which the government foists upon us.
It has been suggested that we could allow our dollar to drop, that we would be far better off to allow that to happen. A drop in the dollar would add to inflation about one-third of a per cent for every 1 per cent drop in the dollar. 1 suppose the truth of the matter is that if we really wanted to manage our economy properly then we could have both a strong dollar and low interest rates.
We all know that the budget of October 28 has been a disaster. Every financial organization from the Economic Council of Canada to the C. D. Howe Institute, every spokesman for every bank and every economic group, has panned that budget. The Economic Council of Canada's analysis of the budget indicated that it caused a 1 per cent rise in inflation alone for 1981. The budget is a disaster. Instead of encouraging energy activity, drilling, construction and encouraging investment into Canada, the budget drives investment out. No wonder our dollar goes down despite high interest rates. If we worked it the other way around, if we encouraged development
February 5, 1981

in Canada, got rid of that energy package or reversed it, and did everything possible from a tax point of view to encourage development which is available in western Canada and the rest of the country, in terms of pipelines in the east and so on, we would be going ahead.
The only thing this government has done so far with respect to its energy package is to make a deal to spend $1.5 billion to pay shareholders of Petrofina $120 per share for shares which six months ago sold for $60. That is what the government has done. Isn't that dandy? My friend says they should have expropriated them at $60 rather than pay $120. And what did they receive? Some 1,100 service stations. Really, that does not make sense. Do we need to buy a bunch of used service stations when we are trying to build Canada?
Only recently the Petrofina station in Lome Park reopened because the company, in desperation, finally turned it over to a local operator for next to nothing in terms of rent. The operator is having a hard time to make any money since nobody wants to buy the product, and there are too many service stations around, anyway. We have all driven around our constituencies and seen those whitewashed service stations. But, what does the government do? It goes out and spends $1.5 billion to buy a bunch of used service stations. That is stupid.
There are many things the government should be doing. It should be encouraging new investment. What is the use of paying the Belgians $120 a share for assets which are already here? If they really wanted some service stations, why not build new ones? It would create some employment. But, what does the government give us? Nothing but a bunch of used service stations.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext: You know as well as we do that we are buying a stream of future benefits. You are saying future benefits are not worth it. We say they are.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
The parliamentary secretary is talking about future benefits. I think the future benefits for most people in Canada should take the form of more jobs and higher pay packets-in terms of real value in their pay packets tomorrow than they have today. The assurance of the past four years, to most people, has been that their purchasing power for the same amount of work and effort has been less and less. Indeed, on average, Canadians probably slipped behind very close to 4 per cent in 1980.
The government must reduce its borrowing requirements, and it cannot be done by buying new service stations and borrowing money at 17 per cent or 17.5 per cent. The government must learn to better manage its accounts and not to borrow as much. What bothers me is the quantum of the debt requirements of this government for new money every year. The requirements in the budget were approximately $11 billion, and it was indicated that the requirements would be less for next year. That is not good enough, but it is good. However, I fear that in fact this will not be the case.
Borrowing Authority
The problem is that the government's borrowing is beginning to crowd out the private entrepreneur, people who wish to take out mortgages and others, in terms of their ability to borrow money. When the government goes to the financial market it is with the highest possible credit rating, at least in its own country, although that may not be the case abroad. When the government goes to the financial market and is prepared to offer 17 per cent for money, as is the case with this government, it forces those persons who need money to match or better the government.
These people who must better or meet the government's ability to borrow in the marketplace are eventually crowded out. As the governor of the Bank of Canada has said, there is no limit as to how much the government will pay-it has a printing press and is able to pay. The effect of the government's willingness to pay these high rates of interest is that it crowds out business and development, and we end up with an economy which performs at less than its potential. As the Economic Council of Canada indicated at page 63 of its report:
There has been no evidence that this has happened,-
It was referring to the crowding out.
-but lenders have insisted on shorter duration agreements and new instruments with extendable terms. This means that the government must refinance a larger portion of its debt each year and thus it may face a debt management problem.
As a result, the government goes further into debt, crowds out other forms of investment, and deals more and more in the short term because people have no confidence in it all the time absorbing all the available money in the system. The result of the enormous deficit and borrowing requirements authorized by this bill is that it puts jobs and the hopes of Canadians in serious jeopardy.
I should like to speak for a moment about what I perceive to be some of the problems. I hope the task force committee which will be looking at the financial arrangements between the federal government and the provinces will become involved with some of these problems. In my view the most serious problem in this country is set out in the report of the Economic Council of Canada:
A good part of the persistent federal deficit can be attributed to below potential performance. Moreover, because the resource royalties and surplus on the Canada and Quebec Pension Plans, the combined deficit of all governments in Canada is expected to be replaced by a surplus . . . However, it is the large federal deficit, rather than the over-all government sector-
This is the cause of the problems of the federal government.
Because the federal government carries out the equalization system in Canada and because it has become involved in matters which constitutionally belong to the provinces-and as a result it no longer has the resources or other revenues to balance out-obviously it becomes necessary for the federal government to reduce its expenditures. The first step of the government should be to cease its involvement in matters of provincial concern.
Throughout the 1960s and 1970s this government entered into one field after another which, by virtue of the British North America Act, were within the competence of provincial

February 5, 1981
Borrowing Authority
governments. An hon. member from the New Democratic Party spoke this afternoon about medicare. While it is great to have a national standard, the operations of hospitals and medical services clearly fall within the scope of the provinces.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext: Are you against medicare?

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
Of course not, but who must pay for it? Part of the expense must be transferred to the provinces in order to stop this federal borrowing. Let us let the provinces handle some of the problems they should have handled all along.
We in this Parliament have a tendency of wanting to get into every act in the country. For example, the budget of the minister responsible for CMHC for this year is in excess of $1.3 billion. I am not against housing-and governments have certain responsibilities with regard to housing-but does the federal government have any responsibility in the area of housing? I have heard members of this House, including some of my colleagues from Vancouver, cry about the housing problems in that city. The province of British Columbia is well off and can look after its own housing problems; it does not need to come to the federal government for assistance. This government should stick to the areas in which it performs well and not go into areas of provincial jurisdiction, because it merely gets into the position of needing to borrow more money.
As the result of the government's involvement in matters of provincial jurisdiction, the bureaucracy grows larger and the financial markets of the country become upset. The Economic Council of Canada suggested that the provinces, because of their resource potential and their methods of taxation, should have access to revenue and should have surplus revenue. We all know, when a government has surplus revenue, that the funds quickly disappear into new social programs and more government.
The problem with which the task force will have to deal is that equalization goes to the root of the federal deficit and, to some extent, to the root of our constitution. This problem should be attended to and solved immediately. When we talk about constitutional patriation, we must also look at the revenue or the dollar and cents end of the matter. It is absolutely foolhardy for provinces, with their surpluses or their easily-carried deficits, to be able to expand their programs while the federal government is requesting borrowing authority for $14 billion.
The government has gotten itself into a backward mess. It has become involved in fields in which it does not belong. However, the government is remaining in those fields, is trying to borrow money, is upsetting the entire interest market in Canada, is crowding out private borrowers and is upsetting the mortgage and business investment markets. It will not get down to the brass tacks of understanding where its responsibilities and those of the provinces lie.
I am glad this task force has been appointed. It will bring to the attention of the House the place where the responsibilities of this government begin and end.
In the couple of minutes that I have left, I should like to return to some of the provisions in the budget and to compare them with what could have been done to get Canada going again and to bring interest rates down, so that the country could grow and federal tax revenues would be more buoyant.
Last year's Crosbie budget contained a provision relating to registered retirement savings plans. If those plans had invested their funds in stock market equities and a capital gain was made, it would have been taxed as a capital gain when the plans were dissolved and not as income as is the case at present. That measure would have encouraged more Canadians to enter the equity market and would have lessened the debt field. It would have had the tendency of keeping rates down considerably, at the same time as providing equity capital for the burgeoning commercial activities that need frontend money in Canada. That provision is not included in the present budget, and that is one of the reasons we do not have the growth that we need to support our dollar and to avoid continually raising interest rates and bringing money into the country to finance debt.
There is the question of the capital gains tax itself. Recently, the government issued a white paper or a pink paper on capital gains taxes. This paper attempts to justify the capital gains tax. I was surprised that the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) did not comment on the paper as, prior to his election to Parliament, he made many comments regarding capital gains. He said the tax was ridiculous, wasteful and harmful but he has not commented on this paper. 1 would be interested to see the government do what it should-bring that paper before the finance committee where it could be discussed and the justification for capital gains tax examined.
I know that one of my colleagues would like to speak before five o'clock, Mr. Speaker, so I will conclude my remarks.

Mr. Speaker, I did not want to cut off the hon. member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) or the very interesting debate that was going on. The hon. member's comments have been most incisive, and I certainly want to associate myself with them. I think his description of the package before us and the performance of this government as a bit of a horror show was most apt.
The $14 billion borrowing authority that the government is asking Parliament to approve must be examined against the background of successive budgetary deficits. On page 43 of the budget document presented to the House on October 28, it is shown that for the past four years the accumulation of budgetary deficits amounts to some $40.1 billion. The projected figure for the next four years for the total anticipated budgetary deficit is $51.8 billion. That is almost $92 billion in budgetary deficits which have accumulated over a period of eight years. That clearly shows a government out of control, and I think most Canadians would find those figures incredible and shocking.
We are not capitalizing on the production potential of the country; instead we are following a philosophy of trying to borrow ourselves rich. We are not stimulating the economy or the production capacity of the country so that it can support
Department of Public Works
expensive government programs. This is very disturbing. We are mortgaging our future and placing an almost impossible burden on our children and our children's children.
The hon. member for Mississauga South spoke of the country's net debt. By March our gross national debt will exceed $120 billion and the net debt will exceed some $80 billion. The interest on that debt is in excess of $12 billion annually. We are spending $1 in $4 on interest on that debt.

DEPARTMENT OF PUBLIC WORKS Mr. Hal Herbert (Vaudreuil) moved:
That an order of the ttouse do issue for a copy of the document prepared in or before October. 1970, which was either submitted to cabinet or prepared for submission to cabinet and which dealt with the restructuring of the Department of Public Works including the option to form it into a Crown corporation.

February 5, 1981
Department of Public Works
He said: Mr. Speaker, I will readily admit that my motive in putting this motion on the Order Paper was not to get production of the document referred to since I was already aware of its content. However, I believed it would give me an opportunity once again to shed some further light on a difficulty I have been working on over the years. 1 refer to the continuing duplication of efforts in various departments. This afternoon I want to discuss specifically property management and construction work as it applies to the public service.
The parliamentary secretary mentioned that the document was a cabinet paper. I might take issue with that. As far as I am aware, it never got to the cabinet table. I suspect it was just a presentation for the approval of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). As I understand the story, this document was presented at the time of the October crisis in 1970, and as a result, it was put away for the time being. Eleven years later, we are still talking about what was proposed in 1970 and what still has not been done in 1980.
My original interest in this subject predates my entry into the House of Commons in 1972. I must admit that, as a construction man, in those days I was somewhat concerned about the efficiency, or lack of efficiency, in the Department of Public Works. I was anxious to find out for myself just what the situation was in that department. To put the parliamentary secretary at rest, I am not going to be too critical of the department this afternoon. In fact, I have been suggesting all along that the problem is that this department has not had a full opportunity to take over, as was proposed in 1970, complete control of construction activity and property management in the public service. It was not until 1975 that I started to put case files together. The more I did so, the more concerned I became.
It may be advisable to say a few words about the department by way of introduction. The Department of Public Works provides accommodation and related realty services to government departments and agencies. These services include construction of buildings, purchase and disposal of land and other real property, rental of premises and the maintenance, improvement and operation of properties owned or leased by the Government of Canada. In addition, on request the department supplies government departments and agencies with technical and construction management services for capital projects.
In his report, the Auditor General commented that there are two principal systems in planning for the acquisition of space. The planning and control system is used to plan the department's internal resource requirements based on projected work load. In order to be fully effective as a foundation for departmental planning and forecasting, the planning and control system must be linked to an extensive data base which includes cost inventory and other operating data. This data base has not been fully developed. Furthermore, actual expenditures were not being systematically compared to plans or budgets to determine the quality of the original plans, nor could changes in the level of funding be related to changes in resources required for individual projects.
The Auditor General concluded that the management of eight of nine projects examined did not demonstrate a reasonable standard of due regard for economy.
Among the Auditor General's recommendations, one can read that the role of the Department of Public Works and its program objectives should be clarified. The department commented on the recommendations and agreed with this one. For the past several years the department has been seeking approval for a modified role and mandate in the context of proposals concerning the rationalization of real property operations in the federal government. I might add that in place of "the past several years", one should read "a minimum of 14 years". In fact, in these short remarks, in which I can only lightly gloss over the problem, I shall be talking of the history of the past 17 years.
The Glassco proposals of some 17 years ago created considerable interest in reform. In 1964, a committee of senior public servants was convened to review the proposals and to make recommendations to ministers. The Glassco commission singled out for special mention the fact that real property activities had become diffused among a large number of departments. It suggested that the Department of Public Works should be made responsible for the planning and supervision of all construction required by civil departments and agencies.
As I said earlier, while I obviously have a few criticisms of the department to make, the reason I mention these and put them on the record is because I have felt all along that these criticisms are being used as excuses by other departments which have not, for various reasons, wanted to co-operate in this exercise of developing for the Government of Canada a single construction company.
Looking at some figures, we see that the Department of Transport from 1975 to 1977 carried out construction amounting to $160 million to $180 million a year.
In the Post Office Department-and this was looked after by the Department of Public Works-construction activity in those same years was running at $50 million to $75 million a year. 1 mention this because with the Post Office becoming a Crown corporation, it is possible that this construction workload may be taken away from the Department of Public Works.
I want to refer to the Department of National Defence; construction in those same years ranged from $50 million to $70 million per year. This work, of course, was carried out by Defence Construction (1951) Limited. I will say right now that if I had any criticism to make of any construction department, it would be DCL.
My reasons there are best illustrated by the construction work that was carried out at the St. Jean military base in Quebec. Construction figures for 1976-77 were $14 million; for 1978, $36 million; and 1978-79, $27 million. Sixteen contractors on that site had extras or additional amounts added to their contracts exceeding 20 per cent of their original signed contracts. That construction exercise at St. Jean, as everyone knows, went considerably over budget. Whether that
February 5, 1981

was justified or not, I believe all construction work should be under the same set of rules and regulations.
It is extremely difficult for the construction industry to cope with the varying tendering methods of various departments, the Ministry of Transport, the Ministry of National Defence and, rather strangely, the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development which gets into the construction act as does, for example, the Department of Veterans Affairs.
I have put on the record before and I should like to mention again, that I saw absolutely no reason why the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development should be building some steps on the east corner of the Parliament Buildings. I inquired the reason why that department was building them and was told at that time that department was responsible for the canal which belonged to Parks Canada, which in turn is part of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. I want to put on the record once again that those steps down to the canal cost us over $500,000, and $500,000 to me represents something like $1,000 a week in interest alone to walk down those stone steps. I suggest that work should better have been done by the Department of Public Works, where it would have been publicly tendered.
Back in 1969 the mood was to change the Department of Public Works into a Crown corporation. 1 do not support that particular proposal. I believe that situation now has been put aside, and I doubt there is any inclination to make it into a Crown corporation. I am not sure that would resolve any problems at all.
The deputy minister at that time, who was put into his job by the Prime Minister with the specific responsibility for reorganization of the Department of Public Works, was Mr. John MacDonald, who today, in 1981, is the chairman of the Tariff Board court. He was saying that the responsibility of the proposed new corporation-whether one talks of a Crown corporation or a reorganized Department of Public Works is unimportant-would include the integration of the existing Defence Construction Limited. Twelve years ago it was being suggested that Defence Construction Limited should be wound up in its present form.
I received a rather interesting answer to a question I put on the Order Paper in connection with Defence Construction Limited. I must admit I found it rather amusing and I should like to read it. I was asking why the work of Defence Construction Limited could not be equally well carried out by the Department of Public Works, and the answer contained the phrase:
"Each time this matter was considered it was agreed that in order to meet the objectives of the Department of National Defence a quick response capability was required."
Of course, I could not resist the temptation then to ask a question as to why the Department of Public Works was unable to provide a quick response capability. "The decision", they say in the answer, "did not imply that the Department of
Department of Public Works
Public Works was unable to provide a quick response capability." In fact, I think wc had a bit of a runaround on that one.
I notice in the estimates for the year just concluded-and I assume this week we are to see the new figures-that the Department of Public Works budget is presently at $754 million, and I believe in supplements there was another $1 million added. In any event, the total for the year is some $755 million. That is quite a sum of money. In fact, if one adds the construction activities of Transport, National Defence and so on, one comes to a sum in excess of $1 billion.
The problem back in 1970 was one which is continually being experienced in our public service, the initialling of some agreement between deputy ministers and then changing position. At that particular time the two deputy ministers concerned were Mr. Simon Reisman, who was secretary of the Treasury Board, and John MacDonald to whom I have already referred. They were in essential agreement on the direction in which we were to be going.
However, the usual forms of delay were brought in, additional task forces were put into operation, additional studies were required, and then in 1970 Simon Reisman became deputy minister of finance. His place as secretary of the Treasury Board was taken by Mr. A. W. Johnson.
Reisman had expressed strong support for the MacDonald proposals from the very beginning and, indeed, with regard to several major points, had urged similar action upon the Department of Public Works previous deputy minister through 1968 and 1969. That, of course, was prior to the appointment of Mr. MacDonald who was sent there for the express purpose of reorganization.
There then obviously was some reluctance on the part of Treasury Board to proceed. I found it quite interesting that just a couple of months ago, on going through the minutes of a meeting of the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture, the same Mr. Johnson appeared as a witness, that is, Mr. Johnson who is now the president of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Let me quote him as follows:
I want to say something about my own preoccupation with efficiency because I really want to make it clear to the committee how strongly I feel about efficiency.
He went on to state:
I reflected a great deal ... on the line of questioning about the comprehensive audit and efficiency.
He went on to state:
My interest in this field goes back a long way. My first five years in government were spent doing efficiency studies. I appeared on a platform with James Macdonell-
That was our last Auditor General.
-and with Walter Gordon, who was then in the consulting business in 1952. 1 published an article on efficiency in government and business in 1962... As Secretary of the Treasury Board here in Ottawa, I was responsible for supervising the experimentation that was being done in the field of PPBS which has now got the new name of "Efficiency and Effectiveness".
He then said:
I do favour a comprehensive audit in the field of economy and efficiency.
